doc.title: Frank Capp interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995

title: Jazz as America's heritage and its audience abroad
summary: Capp says jazz is America's heritage but draws far larger crowds in Japan and Europe, and mentions how musicians were revered in Russia.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Yeah, well we feel that this music is such a big part of this country.
It is, it is. Thank God — I could kiss you for saying that. I mean it’s America’s heritage, you know?
Right. You know all the other art forms have come from Europe. That’s why I say about our country — we’ve got a lot of catching up to do in that area.

Well some people have mentioned that when they’ve gone to Europe and the Europeans say to them, you know, your country is very young. And in a way I think some of our problems stem from that, is that we have a ways to go.

You know you can put the greatest marquee together of the greatest jazz stars in this country. And maybe, maybe you’ll get a thousand people. Maybe. Not for sure. You go to Japan, you go to Europe, with that same card, and you’ll have fifty thousand people. Or twenty thousand people. Vastly more than here. People aren’t interested in jazz here, except the few that understand and appreciate it and realize its meaning. And it’s not that difficult to understand. People say they don’t understand it. What’s there to understand? You feel the beat and you feel the rhythm, and well— I don’t want to pontificate here, get on my soapbox when I talk about it. But it’s really unfortunate that — someone told me that this was before the Iron Curtain came down and all that, that in Russia — I’ve never been to Russia, but Benny Goodman went to Russia. And someone said that at that time if you were a musician or an artist, you were revered over there. Whether it be jazz music
or classic music. The musicians made more than the doctors or engineers did. That’s how they appreciated it. But maybe not so now I don’t know. Anyway.
